extracted.intended_audience: institutions of higher education (administrators, Title IX coordinators), legal counsel, and policymakers implementing Title IX regulations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory preamble describing standards and requirements for recipients (colleges and universities) to address sexual harassment, sexual assault, supportive measures, grievance processes, recordkeeping, and related definitions under Title IX and related federal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment protection for offensive speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The Speech Clause protects even so-called low-worth expression; the government cannot ban hateful expression no matter how hurtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting censorship to be 'on the right side of history' ignores the role of commitment to the First Amendment. The Department and commenters stress reliance on constitutional protections (citing Cohen v. California and related commentary). Recipients retain the ability to respond to offensive speech with supportive measures, institutional speech, or programming to foster a welcoming campus climate rather than censoring speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional response to offensive speech (non-censorship tools)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may respond to offensive speech by providing supportive measures to the complainant, responding with institutional speech, or offering programming to improve campus climate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters and the preamble endorse using 'Walk away, don't listen, or respond with more and better speech' and other non-disciplinary responses rather than censoring protected expression. These tools should be considered particularly where speech is constitutionally protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Davis severe/pervasive/objectively offensive standard for actionable student harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: To be actionable under Title IX (as articulated in Davis), harassment must be so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive that it effectively bars the victim's access to an educational opportunity or benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites Davis repeatedly: actionable harassment can include non-physical acts and does not require physical exclusion. Whether harassment meets the Davis standard requires looking at all circumstances; no single factor is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective and objective perspective in evaluating severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct should be evaluated from both a subjective and objective perspective; objective severity judged from reasonable person in the complainant's position considering all circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2001 Guidance and case law (Harris v. Forklift, Oncale v. Sundowner) are cited to support the dual subjective/objective inquiry. The test 'is not, and by its nature cannot be, a mathematically precise test' and 'no single factor is required.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of equal access (Title IX focus) — no physical exclusion required
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff need not show physical exclusion; liability arises when harassment so undermines and detracts from the victim's educational experience that the victim is effectively denied equal access to resources and opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davis describes 'denial of access' variously (depriving victims of access to educational opportunities, effectively denying equal access). The preamble emphasizes that this educational-equivalent standard is distinct but analogous to workplace 'hostile environment' doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'sexual assault' (Clery Act / FBI UCR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.30 incorporates 'Sexual assault' as defined in 20 U.S.C. 1092(f)(6)(A)(v): an offense classified as a forcible or nonforcible sex offense under the FBI Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Clery Act directs recipients to SRS/NIBRS definitions; the FBI transition from SRS to NIBRS (planned Jan 2021) does not change the range of sex offenses covered (rape, sodomy, sexual assault with an object, fondling, statutory rape, incest). See FBI UCR/NIBRS resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 106.30: definitions of key terms (consent, formal complaint, complainant, respondent, sexual harassment)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.30 defines core terms used throughout the regulations, including 'consent' (entry exists in §106.30), 'formal complaint' (document filed by complainant or signed by Title IX Coordinator), and 'complainant'/'respondent' (anyone alleged to be victim/perpetrator of conduct that could constitute sexual harassment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal complaint triggers a §106.45 grievance process; situations where an individual does not view themselves as a 'victim' likely will not result in filing a formal complaint. A person may be a complainant or respondent regardless of whether a formal complaint has been filed or who reported the conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures requirement (§106.44(a) and §106.30 definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: With or without a grievance process, a recipient's response to sexual harassment must include promptly offering supportive measures to the complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.30 defines 'supportive measures' as individualized services provided without fee or charge, designed to restore or preserve equal access to education without unreasonably burdening the other party. Recipients must document the facts or circumstances that render supportive measures appropriate or inappropriate and must retain records for seven years; if supportive measures are not provided, the recipient must document why that response was not clearly unreasonable in light of known circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies obligation after a finding of responsibility (§106.45(b)(1)(i) and §106.45(b)(7)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a respondent is found responsible following a grievance process that complies with §106.45, the recipient must provide remedies to the complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies may consist of individualized services similar to supportive measures but, unlike supportive measures, may be punitive or disciplinary against the respondent and need not avoid burdening the respondent. The Title IX Coordinator is responsible for effective implementation of remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal resolution option (§106.45(b)(9))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may facilitate informal resolution, with the voluntary written consent of both parties, of any formal complaint except those alleging that an employee sexually harassed a student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations permit informal resolution only when both parties voluntarily agree in writing and exclude employee-on-student harassment allegations from informal resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping and documentation retention (§106.45(b)(10)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must create and maintain for seven years records of any actions taken in response to a report or formal complaint of sexual harassment and must document the basis for their conclusion that their response was not deliberately indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision specifies retention for a seven-year period and requires documentation when supportive measures are not provided explaining why non-provision was not clearly unreasonable under the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate indifference standard and deference on sanctions where §106.45 process followed
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations refrain from second-guessing recipients' disciplinary sanctions so long as those sanctions follow an accurate, reliable determination reached through a §106.45 grievance process; Title IX Coordinator decisions to initiate grievances when a complainant does not desire that action will be evaluated under the general deliberate indifference standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients retain flexibility to decide appropriate sanctions when behavior constituted sexual harassment under §106.30 but did not subjectively offend or distress the complainant. A Title IX Coordinator's override of a complainant's wishes is evaluated for clear unreasonableness in light of known circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stalking as sexual harassment if 'on the basis of sex'
rubrics_metrics.description: Stalking constitutes 'sexual harassment' under §106.30 when the stalking is 'on the basis of sex' (for example, when the stalker desires to date the victim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stalking that is not 'on the basis of sex' may not constitute sexual harassment under Title IX but may be prohibited and addressed under a recipient's non-Title IX codes of conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat against overbroad application of harassment policies (protect academic freedom and avoid chilling speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters and cited scholarship criticize misapplication of peer harassment laws and overbroad definitions that have been used to punish constitutionally protected speech, chilling campus discussion and academic freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites numerous examples and scholarly commentary of universities punishing protected speech (e.g., classroom discussions, readings, hypothetical exam questions) and warns that overly broad harassment policies can cause speakers to self-censor and undermine the 'marketplace of ideas.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of trauma variability and evidentiary perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Trauma responses vary across individuals; trauma cannot be identified simply by looking at someone and everyone responds differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites commenters and scholarship (e.g., Rebecca Campbell) to stress that evaluators should account for variability in how individuals respond to trauma when assessing reports and harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for disparate impact and bias in Title IX enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters raised concerns that broad or vague definitions and lowered standards could disproportionately impact minority students (e.g., men of color) in adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites scholarship and journalism noting overrepresentation of certain demographic groups among accused students and warns decisionmakers to be mindful of unconscious bias and systemic disadvantages that could skew outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to cross-authority sources and interplay with other federal statutes (e.g., Title VII, Clery Act, VAWA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory interpretations and standards draw on Title VII case law, the Clery Act definitions, VAWA definitions (dating violence, domestic violence, stalking), and FBI UCR classifications to inform Title IX implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains that Davis relied on Title VII cases for formulating the 'effectively denied equal access' element; Clery Act and VAWA definitions inform what conduct is covered; recipients should be aware of these cross-authority definitions and resources (FBI UCR/NIBRS).
